DOCUMENT NO. 001 / MARCH 12, 2020
THREE
DAYS.
Michigan announced that school buildings would close beginning Monday, March 16, 2020. The initial announcement anticipated reopening April 6. Across the country, millions of families made plans around what they thought might be a short interruption. They did not yet know what was coming.
Source: State of Michigan, March 12, 2020. Timing differed across states and school districts.
01 / What normal felt like

THE LAST
ordinary day.

In 2019, a crowded hallway was background noise. In 2020, the same space could become a public-health problem. Drag the divider. Look at what disappears.

2019 · EVERYBODY HERE
2020 · HALLS EMPTY
↔
← Busy hallwayHalf the school day is gone.Empty building →
School

What vanished?

The crowded lunch table, the bus ride, the team practice, the chance to ask a teacher a question in person.

Work

What kept going?

Hospitals, groceries, warehouses, deliveries, emergency services, and many other essential services could not simply shut down.

Home

What got crowded?

Kitchen tables became classrooms. Bedrooms became workplaces. A single device or internet connection could determine who got to participate.

Scenes are newly generated illustrations, not authentic photographs of any named school or individuals.

02 / The moment nobody knew was historic

IT WAS
SUPPOSED TO BE
TEMPORARY.

The dates below are real. The notice is a classroom reconstruction based on Michigan's March 12 announcement—not an actual school memo.

STATE OF MICHIGAN / SCHOOL CLOSURE NOTICE · RECONSTRUCTION
THURSDAY, MARCH 12, 2020

All K–12 school buildings will close to students beginning Monday, March 16. The original closure window extends through April 5, with a planned April 6 reopening.

Students: Take home the materials you may need. Families and educators: further guidance will follow.

WHAT NO ONE COULD PUT IN THIS NOTICE: HOW LONG IT WOULD LAST.

03 / The chain reaction

THE DAYS
kept changing.

This wasn't one shutdown button. It was a sequence of decisions, discoveries, illnesses, and uneven experiences. Select a date to investigate.

THE FIRST SIGNS

Before anyone knew

20
Important distinction: A pandemic means widespread transmission across countries. It does not mean every person faced the same medical risk, and calling an outbreak a pandemic did not itself order schools closed.

THE STUDENT

THE QUESTION THIS PERSON FACES

WHO ELSE PAYS THE PRICE?

WHAT THIS TEACHES US

94% of surveyed U.S. parents with school-age children reported their child’s school was closed in April 2020.
21% of surveyed parents with children learning from home anticipated difficulty completing schoolwork because of no computer access.
29% anticipated their child would need to do schoolwork on a cellphone.

These percentages are from an April 7–12, 2020 Pew Research Center survey of U.S. adults with school-age children, not counts of every U.S. student. Study and methodology ↗

05 / Learn the invisible math

HOW CAN ONE
BECOME MANY?

The scary part of an outbreak is what can happen before anyone realizes it is spreading. Experiment with the average number of new infections caused by a newly infected person over one hypothetical generation.

HYPOTHETICAL TRANSMISSION PER GENERATION
1.8
Growing fast
LESS SPREAD · 0.6MORE SPREAD · 2.4
What does it teach? When transmission stays above one in this simple example, each generation becomes larger. Below one, each becomes smaller. Real epidemics also depend on immunity, timing, contact patterns, testing, variants and many other factors. This is a teaching illustration, not a COVID case forecast or medical model.
The reason behind precautions

Slow the peak.

Officials sought to reduce transmission so fewer people needed hospital care at the same time. Buying time could help staff, supplies and treatments catch up. Measures brought benefits and costs; their effects depended on how and where they were used.

The part a graph cannot show

Every bar represents people.

Among the stakes were medical workers, families afraid of infection, workers losing income, students missing school, and patients waiting for non-COVID care. A chart is useful; it is never the entire story.

06 / The human and economic cost

THE NUMBERS
had addresses.

Numbers describe the scale. They cannot explain a kitchen table with an empty chair or what it felt like to lose a paycheck overnight.

A real concern

Protecting public health

Rapid spread threatened lives and hospital capacity. Some people favored restrictions, vaccination, testing, and precautions as tools to reduce harm—particularly for older adults and people facing high medical risk.

Also a real concern

Protecting everyday life

School disruption, isolation, lost jobs, disrupted childcare and limits on gatherings carried real costs. People debated how long restrictions should last, which were justified, and who should bear the burden.

Think like a historian: Do not judge every 2020 decision using information people only learned months or years later. But do examine what evidence officials had, how it changed, and who was affected.

CHANGE ONE
decision.

History could have unfolded differently—but alternate history is not a cheat code. Choose a change, then consider what it might improve, what problems would remain, and what we cannot know.

POSSIBLE ALTERNATE HISTORY

09 / The legacy, in your life

2026 IS NOT
2019.

Some changes stuck. Others faded or remain contested. These are examples students can recognize without pretending everyone had the same pandemic.

Education

What is “being in class”?

Video calls and online assignments became familiar even as in-person school resumed. The pandemic also intensified attention to interrupted learning and unequal technology access.

Work

Where is the workplace?

Many jobs learned to operate remotely or with hybrid arrangements. Other jobs—healthcare, retail, production—still demanded an in-person presence.

Healthcare

How do we treat illness?

Telehealth, vaccine research, infection precautions, and long-COVID care became more visible parts of public discussion.

Family

Who did we lose time with?

Missed reunions, graduations, funerals, and ordinary time together remain part of millions of family stories.

Government

Who decides during an emergency?

Public debates about emergency powers, personal choice, school closures and trust in institutions continued long after the immediate crisis.

History

Did the pandemic “end”?

The U.S. federal COVID-19 public health emergency declaration ended May 11, 2023. That did not mean the virus vanished, or that all its effects were over.

Source for the emergency ending: CDC archived guidance, 2023 ↗
